title: When Selecting Between Internal and External Candidates Give the Insider the Edge
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece weighs the tradeoffs between hiring internal versus external candidates for critical roles, acknowledging the genuine appeal of outsiders — fresh ideas, no legacy politics, and a signal of serious organizational change. But it argues leaders should still favor internal candidates in a roughly even race because the internal candidate's weaknesses are fully known while an external hire's flaws remain uncertain even after reference checks. The piece proposes a concrete rule of thumb: an external candidate must be a full step higher in experience, knowledge, and skill to justify the added risk. It closes by noting outside hires often do meet that higher bar, but the burden of proof should sit with them.
points: External candidates offer genuine advantages: fresh perspective, faster execution, and freedom from legacy politics.
Internal candidates carry known weaknesses, while an external hire's flaws remain uncertain even after background checks.
The recommended rule of thumb: external candidates must be a full step higher in experience and skill to win an even race.
Internal selection rewards continuity and loyalty but shouldn't override genuinely superior outside talent.
quotes: When selecting talent for a critical position, leaders often evaluate talent from inside and outside the organization.
External hires often promote change and execute faster than an internal candidate.
But for all the outsider’s advantages, good leaders wisely give an edge to internal talent.
There are no optimal candidates without flaws and skill tradeoffs.
The best leaders operate from a rule of thumb: To be selected, the external candidate must be one full step higher in experience, knowledge, and skill than the internal candidate.
By giving an edge to the internal candidate, externals must meet a higher bar. The best news is that they often do.
